extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners (and practitioners) on interpreting claim language and determining definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (and pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph), including application of the broadest reasonable interpretation, means‑plus‑function analysis, recordkeeping, and resolution procedures (interviews, office actions, reasons for allowance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, a claim must be given its broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification because the applicant can amend claims during prosecution and BRI reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be interpreted more broadly than justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz, Buszard. Focus inquiry on what would be reasonable from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art. See MPEP § 2111 for full discussion. Examiners apply BRI in prosecution (different from post‑issuance court construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning / ordinary and customary meaning of claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of the claim must be given their plain meaning—the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention—unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources evidencing ordinary meaning include the claims, specification, drawings, and prior art; the specification is the best source and may serve as a glossary. The presumption of ordinary meaning may be rebutted only by a clear and intentional special definition in the specification (In re Morris). Applicants may not add a special definition after filing (but may point to a definition already in the filed specification). See MPEP § 2111.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of claim interpretation, examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA 112, sixth paragraph). If invoked, the limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Donaldson Co., and MPEP § 2181 I for more information regarding determining invocation and corresponding structure for means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand difference between prosecution (BRI) and court claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented claims are not given BRI during court proceedings; courts apply the Nautilus definiteness standard (claims must inform skilled artisans about scope with reasonable certainty). The Office construes claims using BRI to develop a clear prosecution record and to facilitate sharpening and clarifying claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Packard, Morris, Zletz, Buszard. Applicant can amend claims or provide persuasive explanations/evidence to show clarity. Examiners should not conflate court standards with examination practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision for definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the statutory threshold requirements of clarity and precision in 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph), not whether more suitable language exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow some latitude in expression provided statutory requirements are satisfied. If patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims define it with required particularity and distinctness, allow them. Examiners may suggest language improvements but should not insist on personal preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the‑circumstances analysis: three primary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of: (A) the content of the particular application disclosure; (B) the teachings of the prior art; and (C) the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must consider these factors together rather than in isolation when determining compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole and the notice function
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing a claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b), the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and serves the notice function required by the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Solomon v. Kimberly‑Clark and In re Larsen: the totality of claim limitations and their interactions determine what the inventor contributed; claims must notify the public what is within and outside patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness arises when more than one reasonable interpretation exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person of ordinary skill, reading the claim (under BRI) in light of the specification, would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph) is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners cautioned not to confuse breadth with indefiniteness: a broad claim can be definite if its scope is clearly defined (genus vs unclear genus examples). See MPEP § 2173.05(h) for Markush issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a prima facie indefiniteness rejection, the examiner should clearly communicate in the Office action the specific findings and reasons supporting the rejection and avoid mere conclusory statements that the claim is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 706.03 and § 707.07(g). Provide detailed explanation of why the term/phrase renders the metes and bounds unclear and, whenever practicable, indicate how the issue may be resolved. Examples and fact‑specific rationales appear in MPEP § 2173.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit a meaningful response
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office action should identify the specific term/phrase that is indefinite and explain why the metes and bounds are unclear so the applicant can meaningfully respond (explain/submit evidence or amend the claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant fails to adequately respond to the prima facie case, the examiner may make the indefiniteness rejection final (Packard). Cite Halliburton, Morton Intl. Examiners should point out specifics and suggest ways to resolve the indefiniteness where practicable. See MPEP § 707.07(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid per se rules; use fact‑specific rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections for indefiniteness; examples of indefinite language are fact‑specific and should not be applied as per se rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2173.05(d) for examples; analyze each case on its facts rather than applying blanket prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness before rejecting when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, examiners are encouraged to attempt resolution through an interview with the applicant or representative before issuing a rejection, as interviews can clarify BRI, meaning of limitations, preamble scope, means‑plus‑function invocation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any interview substance must be made of record (MPEP § 713.04; 37 CFR 1.2). After interviews, make record entries explaining why discussed terms are or are not sufficiently clear, whether they invoke 112(f), corresponding structures identified, and any amendments discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in Reasons for Allowance when record is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prosecution record as a whole does not make clear reasons for allowance, the examiner may set forth the claim interpretation applied in Reasons for Allowance under 37 CFR 1.104(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice improves quality and reliability of issued patents. Before allowance, examiner may specify allowable subject matter and reasons. Ensure statements do not place unwarranted interpretations on the claims. See MPEP § 1302.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should serve as a glossary; correspondence between specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ideally serves as a glossary to claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) so meaning is ascertainable by reference to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not provide needed support/antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1). Applicant may be required to amend the description to provide support (without introducing new matter) or amend the claim. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181 IV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict or inconsistency between claim and specification renders claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is clear on its face may nonetheless be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency with the specification disclosure renders the scope uncertain (internal inconsistency makes claim indefinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Moore, In re Cohn, In re Hammack, In re Anderson examples where specification‑claim conflicts caused indefiniteness. No claim may be read independently of its supporting disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not indefiniteness; address undue breadth under proper statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth alone does not equal indefiniteness. A claim can be broad yet definite if its boundaries are clearly delineated. Undue breadth should be addressed under the statutory provision appropriate to the reason it is too broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If too broad because it does not set forth what inventor regards as the invention (evidence outside filed application) → reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). If too broad because not supported or enabling → reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If too broad because it reads on prior art → reject under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: New terminology must have apparent meaning from specification or prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at filing. New terms are permitted but must be made clear and precise so metes and bounds are ascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification states the intended meaning for a term, that meaning controls for examination (In re Zletz). Use MPEP § 2181 when new terms implicate means‑plus‑function issues.
